scorecard.title: Scorecard: how accurate, and how precise
scorecard.body: Scored only on the checks nothing in the model was set on. Bias is the model over the record on average — 1.00× is unbiased, 0.10× ten times too low — and scatter how far single events stray from that average, in natural-log units. For death tolls, inside is the claim of the 9-in-10 band, which should hold about nine records in ten while being as narrow as it can; band is how wide it is, in orders of magnitude. For waves and eruption columns, inside only means accepted. Each family is scored as a whole and by size, because a scenario you build asks how good the model is near its own inputs.
scorecard.note: Bias and scatter need two checks where both the model and the record are above zero, and mean little below five. Zeros are counted apart in the full report, which also scores every check, fitted ones included.

byRule.title: Held out by rule: every event a database holds
byRule.body: A handful of held-out checks can be a lucky handful, and a list is only as fair as whoever wrote it. So two sets were chosen by a rule and committed before the model saw any of them: every earthquake of magnitude 6 or more and up to 40 km deep in NOAA's significant-earthquake database from 2008 to 2025 — {{earthquakes}} of them — and every eruption phase since 2009 in the IVESPA database — {{plumes}}. Nothing was tuned on them, and nothing is left out of the full report: every row, and every miss.
byRule.earthquakes: Earthquake death tolls, held out by rule
byRule.plumes: Eruption columns, held out by rule

table.inside: Inside, where there is something to hold

byRule.note: Inside counts only the events where the record or the band is above zero: {{zeros}} earthquakes killed nobody where the model's band also said nobody, which is inside by construction and would flatter the count. Without the {{seen}} earthquakes already checked above: bias {{bias}}, inside {{inside}} of {{rows}}. The database admits the earthquakes that did damage, so the quiet ones, where a false alarm would show, are few.

tolls.title: Death tolls against events that were counted
tolls.body: Each event is run through the same casualty model the simulator uses, on the population maps it ships. The band is where nine in ten of 200 plausible versions of the event land — a claim that can be wrong. A gated row stops a release if its band ever stops containing the record; the others are measured and shown with their cause.

validation.causesBody: No miss is left without a named cause — the software refuses to build otherwise. These are the causes, each once, with the events it explains.

evacuation.label: People had left
evacuation.body: The model counts everyone who lived inside the footprint. At Mount St Helens the mountain had been closed for two months; at Pinatubo sixty thousand people were evacuated before the climax. A model that counts everyone who lived there cannot reach a toll made by everyone having left — and this error only ever runs high, never low.

buildingStock.label: The buildings were not the ones the curve was made for
buildingStock.body: Deaths from shaking use the fatality curve USGS PAGER fitted for each country, and most countries have no curve of their own and borrow their region's. Amatrice killed 299 in medieval stone villages that fare far worse than Italy's average building, and Gorkha killed in the brick of the Kathmandu valley. Held out, Christchurch killed 185 where the curve New Zealand borrows reads a handful even at the strongest shaking, and Pohang killed nobody where the one South Korea borrows reads 35. A curve made for a country or a region can be wrong for the buildings it is applied to, in both directions.

populationRaster.label: The population map is coarser than the blast
populationRaster.body: At Beirut the most lethal ring is 240 m across — twenty times smaller than a cell of the population map the tests can read. The model spreads the city's average density over a port basin where nobody lives. The finer map the live site uses would see the difference; no offline test can reach it.

drownedOffline.label: They drowned, and the tests have no sea floor
drownedOffline.body: More than nine in ten of Tōhoku's and Sumatra's dead were killed by the tsunami. The wave needs real sea-floor data, which only the live site downloads, so these rows count the shaking alone and sit far below the record by construction. The coastal toll is measured separately, in the browser, and documented in the roadmap.

populationChanged.label: The map counts who lives there now
populationChanged.body: Hiroshima held about 350 000 people in 1945 and about 1.2 million today. The population map is from 2020, so the model must overshoot — which is why this row is shown but does not gate, even though it lands inside the record.

occupancy.label: The map counts residents, not who was there at that hour
occupancy.body: Mount St Helens erupted at 08:32 on a Sunday. Its closed zones reached about eight kilometres and the lateral blast went nearly four times further, so the model is right to treat the blast sector as unwarned — only three of the 57 dead were inside the red zone. But it fills that sector from a map of where people live, which puts 586 residents in it, and the blast came into logging land whose crews were not working that day. Held out, Unzen 1991 is the same problem the other way round: the 43 killed by its flow were mostly journalists, firefighters and police inside a valley its residents had been advised to leave, and a map of residents has no way to hold them.

mechanismNotModelled.label: They died of something the model does not simulate
mechanismNotModelled.body: Pinatubo's danger zone had been widened to 40 km and some sixty thousand people had left, so the model now counts the currents over a cleared zone and finds a few dozen dead. Most of the 847 who died were killed by roofs collapsing under ash soaked by a typhoon, and by disease in the evacuation camps — two mechanisms this model does not contain. It misses from below, and for that reason.

belowResolution.label: A handful of deaths is below what a rate can resolve
belowResolution.body: A fatality curve is a rate applied to thousands of people, and it resolves no finer than that. At Kaikōura, held out, the curve New Zealand borrows gives the people near the fault about one death, on a band that reaches thirty, against two recorded: inside, by a death either way. Among the earthquakes held out by rule it is the commonest miss — one to ten dead where the band says none — and each is shown rather than argued away.

footprint.label: The shaking footprint is too large
footprint.body: For a great rupture the intensity rings are a relation for a single point, stretched along the whole fault. On the rings used until 14 September 2026 Tōhoku's shaking alone came to ten times the whole record; on Boore et al. 2014's, adopted that day, it is about 4,500 — three times the deaths the earthquake itself caused — with the area of intensity VIII still two and a half times what USGS measured. The row is inside only because its band spans five orders of magnitude.

waves.title: Waves against measurements
waves.body: Wave heights written down by instruments and surveys: a buoy in the Pacific, a table of heights in a lagoon, deposits on a coast. A height measured from crest to trough is halved, because the model computes how far the crest rises above still water. Model is the figure the tests check, asked of the same law the wave map on the globe uses; On the globe is shown only where a row checks a different number — because a check on a number the globe does not show would be a check on nothing.
waves.globeNote: Where the globe misses a measurement the tests contain: {{list}}. This list is kept empty by the tests, so an entry here is a failure that has to be explained.

footprint.title: Shaking footprint against USGS ShakeMap
footprint.body: How much ground the model shakes at intensity VII, VIII and IX, against the area the US Geological Survey mapped after each earthquake. The model predicts the typical shaking; a real earthquake is one draw of it, and one standard deviation of ground motion already means more than twice the radius. So the fair test is not each row but the whole: is the model centred, and does it scatter no more than the ground does?
footprint.bias: Centred at {{ratio}} in radius — {{se}} standard errors from exactly centred, so the model cannot be shown to be off-centre. Scatter {{sd}}, against the {{expected}} that published ground-motion scatter implies. That is a ceiling: over an area part of the scatter averages out, and the part that moves a whole earthquake at once implies {{between}}.
footprint.biasOff: Centred at {{ratio}} in radius — {{se}} standard errors from exactly centred: the model is off-centre. Scatter {{sd}}, against the {{expected}} that published ground-motion scatter implies. That is a ceiling: over an area part of the scatter averages out, and the part that moves a whole earthquake at once implies {{between}}.
footprint.invented: Painted at an intensity the earthquake never reached: {{list}}. A laboratory-level model has none; this list can only get shorter.

interpolation.title: How much the population shortcut costs
interpolation.body: The live site cannot count the population two hundred times per scenario, so it counts it at a handful of rings and reads the rest off the curve between them. The tests can afford the exact count at every radius. Comparing the two is how we know the band on the site is about the event and not about the shortcut.
interpolation.tooFewLow: too few dead at the low end to compare it
interpolation.worst: Worst comparable end: {{factor}}×, against a limit of 2×.

anchors.title: Where the model has been measured
anchors.body: Every event the model is checked against, by family, and what was measured about it. Gated quantities stop a release if the model drifts; declared ones are measured and shown with a reason. When you run a scenario, the simulator tells you how far it sits from the nearest of these.

gaps.title: What the model does not do
gaps.body: Stated here so nobody has to discover it.

evacuation.item: A warned coast evacuates on a timer, not on the shaking
evacuation.note: Volcanic scenarios now carry the zone that was cleared. For tsunamis the model still gives a warning no effect with under half an hour of lead — and on Tōhoku's coast, where most people left within minutes of the shaking, that over-counts the dead about three times. The published evacuation-response data needed to replace the timer is on the roadmap.

farField.item: Distant coasts get too small a wave from very long ruptures
farField.note: Sumatra's far coasts get a wave five to ten times too small, and the cause is not settled. The wave law does not use the length of the fault. In the open ocean it holds: on 113 buoy records of nine great earthquakes at sea, read to rules written before the model was run on them, it is right at the median, where an exact solution for an even slip over the same faults comes out 1.4 times too high. None of the nine faults is as long as Sumatra's. The buoy off Japan it was once tuned on recorded 81 cm, not the 30 this project believed; the model gives it 30 cm.

coastalOffline.item: The coastal toll is not in these tables
coastalOffline.note: It needs real sea-floor data that only the live site downloads; it is measured in the browser and documented in the roadmap.

bandPhysicsOnly.item: The band draws the fatality curve's scatter, but not the census
bandPhysicsOnly.note: Since 14 September the nine-in-ten band redraws the earthquake and, for shaking, how far one earthquake's deaths stray from its country's curve, by the amount USGS PAGER publishes. The population map is still held fixed, and so are the death rates for blasts and pyroclastic currents, which publish no such scatter. PAGER measured its scatter on real shaking maps, so it overlaps with the ground-motion scatter drawn beside it by an amount not separated here. Where a country's curve is steep or uncertain the band spans four orders of magnitude or more, and a record inside it has passed nothing.

greatRupture.item: The largest earthquakes are counted on rings drawn for a single point
greatRupture.note: From magnitude 7.5 the intensity rings are a relation made for a single point, stretched along the whole rupture. Held out by rule, those earthquakes come out about twice their record — fourteen times on the rings used until 14 September 2026 — and their band holds the records by being very wide. A relation fitted to long ruptures and ocean-trench earthquakes is still to come.

inventedShaking.item: The rings paint strong shaking where the ShakeMaps record none
inventedShaking.note: 190 of the 370 USGS ShakeMaps the rings were chosen on hold no ground at intensity VII, and the model draws a VII ring about every one of those earthquakes, on any ground. The rings take no account of how deep an earthquake starts, and a ShakeMap's grid misses a peak smaller than one of its cells; which of the two is responsible is not known. On 809 earthquakes nobody had looked at, an equation that reads the depth painted 298 such bands where the current rings paint 1 374, but lost on the score chosen in advance, which gives no credit for a band rightly left blank. The ground is also one value, read under the epicentre, for the whole footprint, where a ShakeMap reads the ground of each place.

subduction.item: Ocean-trench earthquakes are shaken with rules made for earthquakes on land
subduction.note: The shaking comes from a relation fitted to shallow crustal earthquakes, and for the 2011 earthquake the model paints nearly three times the area of intensity VIII that the ShakeMap recorded. Two more simplifications show on the same event: every fault gets one stiffness of rock, though along a trench it changes with depth, and Tōhoku's fault slips 13 m on average where studies of the earthquake find about 10, because the rupture area taken from a published size relation is smaller than theirs.

tunedUnsourced.item: Two wave calibrations rest on numbers their sources do not give
tunedUnsourced.note: The 2018 collapse of Anak Krakatau was tuned to a wave of about 85 m attributed to a 2019 study that simulates one of nearly 50 m; Storegga to a wave of 5–10 m attributed to a study that measured deposits on the coast. They stay as they are until a number the sources do give is chosen, and are marked here meanwhile.

unread.item: Two numbers have not been checked against their source
unread.note: The tsunami arrival times, whose cited source does not exist, so their tests are switched off; and the depth of large craters, taken from a study of Venus through a later paper that quotes it.

airburstShock.item: An airburst's blast is a point that does not move, drawn as round rings
airburstShock.note: Since 15 September 2026 the blast of an airburst is the one the Earth Impact Effects Program draws, and it matches that program's numbers within 1 %. It treats the burst as a still point. At Chelyabinsk, flown as Popova et al. measured it, 1 kPa, enough to break windows, reaches 30 km (68 km for a moving source), where windows broke over about 10,000 km² — a circle of 56 km; in the city it gives 0.7 kPa where the broken windows say about 3 kPa. At Tunguska its 20 kPa ring is at 11.5 km, against the 26.5 km of flattened forest. A body on a shallow path spreads its energy along the path and damages an ellipse that reaches farthest across it; the only analytic model of that line source does not hold so close to the trail, and the shape has been drawn only by three-dimensional simulations.

explosionProject.item: Parts of the explosion model are this project's, not the book's
explosionProject.note: Burns start at fixed doses of heat, where Glasstone & Dolan make them grow with the size of the weapon; the reach of the initial radiation follows a fit of this project's; the heat a burst radiates between the ground and the air is a straight line between the book's two values; and the death rates for conventional explosions were written with Beirut in view.

volcanoCalibrations.item: The volcanic relations are this project's calibrations
volcanoCalibrations.note: How far pyroclastic currents run, where ash falls, how far lahars travel and how much an eruption cools the climate are set on reference eruptions that the source review of September 2026 did not go back to check. A current is drawn as a disc around the vent: at Fuego in 2018 the model's disc reaches 3.7 km while the current that killed ran 11.7 km down one ravine, and its toll lands inside the record only because the two errors cancel.

impactToll.item: No impact toll can ever be checked
impactToll.note: No asteroid impact in recorded history has killed anyone who was counted. The simulator says so beside every impact toll.

surfaceBurst.item: A burst on the surface of open water makes no wave here.
surfaceBurst.note: Glasstone & Dolan's wave relations are for a burst within the water, at any depth in it, and give nothing for one resting on the surface. So the wave jumps from nothing to the full relation as the charge goes under. Other studies of explosion waves describe surface bursts that do make waves; until a relation is taken from them, the jump stays and is said.

outsideCount.item: Some causes of death are not counted
outsideCount.note: Fallout, initial radiation, famine, disease and climate. For an impact the size of the one that ended the dinosaurs, the climate is what kills most survivors.

validation.footer: Every figure here comes from docs/VALIDATION_REPORT.json, which the software regenerates and checks at every commit.

roles.title: Which checks are validation
roles.body: A check the model was built to pass shows that the fit holds, not that the model is right. For each quantity it checks, every measured event carries one of these roles; the full report says, row by row, what makes it so.

tuned.label: tuned on it
tuned.body: A coefficient, an input or a modelling choice in Nimbus was made with this row in view: set so the quantity comes out as recorded, or chosen because an alternative made the row worse.

inputInferred.label: input from it
inputInferred.body: The scenario's input is itself inferred, in the literature, from the quantity being checked, so the agreement is partly by construction.

sameSource.label: same source
sameSource.body: The published relation the model uses was fitted on data that include this event, or the record is read from a published relation rather than measured at the event.

heldOut.label: held out
heldOut.body: None of these, as far as the code and its cited sources show: an out-of-sample test.

unestablished.label: not established
unestablished.body: Not yet checked; the full report says what is still open.
